title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description: Brute force to optimized: exploring every subset of intervals to keep versus a greedy that sorts by end time and keeps whatever does not conflict.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals that need to be removed so that the rest of the intervals do not overlap.

blocks.text: Given a set of intervals, some of which overlap each other, remove the fewest possible intervals so that none of the remaining ones overlap.

blocks.title: Analogy: Scheduling the Most Non-Conflicting Meetings
blocks.text: Picture a set of proposed meeting times, some conflicting with each other, and needing to cancel the fewest meetings so that every remaining meeting can happen without conflict. Always keeping whichever meeting ends soonest leaves the most room in the schedule for everything that comes after.

blocks.caption: Sorting by end time and always keeping the earliest-ending interval maximizes future room

blocks.text: Removing [1,3] leaves [1,2], [2,3], [3,4], which do not overlap, so 1 removal is enough.
All three intervals are identical and fully overlapping; keeping just one and removing the other two needs 2 removals.

Before trying every possible subset of intervals to remove, notice this is the classic "activity selection" problem in disguise: maximize the number of KEPT intervals, then the removals are just the leftover count.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Minimizing removals is the same as maximizing how many intervals are kept without overlapping.

Observation 2: Sorting intervals by their END time, and greedily keeping an interval whenever it starts at or after the end of the last kept interval, is the well-known optimal strategy for maximizing non-overlapping intervals.

Observation 3: Keeping the interval that ends soonest, among any conflicting group, always leaves at least as much room for future intervals as keeping any other choice.

Observation 4: Every interval that fails this "starts late enough" check must be removed, and counting those failures directly gives the minimum removal count.
This leads to sorting by end time, then greedily keeping intervals that do not conflict with whatever was kept most recently, counting every conflicting one as a removal.

Conceptually, try every possible subset of intervals to remove, and find the smallest one whose remaining intervals do not overlap. Practically demonstrated here as checking every pair for overlap and reasoning about removal counts directly, without the greedy end-time ordering.

items: Consider every possible subset of intervals as "kept," from largest to smallest.
Check whether the kept subset has any overlapping pair.
The first (largest) subset with no overlaps determines the minimum removal count, intervals.length minus that subset's size.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: try every subset of intervals to keep, check for overlaps

codes.python:
def erase_overlap_intervals(intervals):
    n = len(intervals)
    best_kept = 0
    for mask in range(1 << n):                     # every subset of intervals
        kept = [intervals[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i)]
        kept.sort()
        ok = True
        for i in range(1, len(kept)):
            if kept[i][0] < kept[i - 1][1]:          # overlap found
                ok = False
                break
        if ok:
            best_kept = max(best_kept, len(kept))
    return n - best_kept

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every one of the 2 to the n possible subsets of intervals is examined as a candidate "kept" set.
This guarantees the true optimum is found, at the cost of exponential time, only feasible for tiny inputs.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 to the n times n log n), every subset checked, each requiring a sort and overlap scan.
Space: O(n) per subset.
Limitation: completely impractical beyond a handful of intervals; the well-known greedy "sort by end time" strategy achieves the exact same optimum without ever enumerating subsets.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why exploring every subset is unnecessary: this is exactly the classical activity selection problem, maximize non-overlapping intervals kept, which has a well-known greedy optimal strategy.

What is the greedy rule: sort intervals by their END time; walk through them, keeping an interval whenever its start is at or after the end of the most recently kept interval, otherwise discarding (removing) it.

Why does sorting by END time (not start time) work: keeping the interval that finishes earliest, among any group of conflicting intervals, always leaves the most possible room for intervals that come later.

The core idea: sort by end time, greedily keep non-conflicting intervals, and count every discarded one as a removal.

Sort intervals by their end time. Track the end of the most recently kept interval, starting at negative infinity. For each interval in sorted order, if its start is at or after that tracked end, keep it and update the tracked end; otherwise, it conflicts and must be removed, incrementing the removal count.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: sort by end time, greedily keep non-conflicting intervals

blocks.text: Sorting by end time and always keeping the interval that finishes soonest is provably optimal for maximizing kept non-overlapping intervals: any other choice among conflicting intervals would end no earlier, leaving no more (and possibly less) room for subsequent intervals. Since removals are exactly the intervals that fail this greedy keep-check, counting them directly gives the true minimum.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(1) extra, or O(log n) to O(n) depending on the sort implementation.

blocks.text: Non-overlapping Intervals is the classic activity selection problem: sorting by end time and greedily keeping non-conflicting intervals maximizes what is kept, and minimizing removals is just the complement of that same greedy process.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "why sort by end time and not start time", think: keeping whichever interval finishes soonest always leaves the most room for everything after it.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in exponential time; the optimized greedy runs in O(n log n) time, dominated by sorting.

items: Pattern: classical activity selection, sort by end time, greedily keep non-conflicting intervals.
Core Idea: always keep the interval finishing soonest among any conflicting group, since it leaves the most room for future intervals; count every interval that fails this check as a removal.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized greedy.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(1) extra for the optimized greedy.
Most Important Observation: minimizing removals is the same as maximizing kept intervals, solved optimally by sorting on END time.
Interview Difficulty: a standard, well-known greedy once the end-time sort insight is recognized.
One line memory trick: sort by end time, keep what fits, remove what conflicts.
